zh.title: 之一 · 反对是他自己要来的
zh.deck: 请来的反对者越有分量，作者越能从他们没有反对的地方读出消息。

paragraphs: 次序本来可以是这样：书先印出来，有人不服，写书来驳，作者再答，一来一回好几年，散在好几本书里。
这本书没走这条路。反对是在付印之前就要来的。

sections.heading: 一封开篇就抱怨的信
paragraphs: 第四组反驳出自阿尔诺。他那一组是从一封给梅森的信开头的，头一句就是抱怨。
您不肯白白给我好处，他写道，您索一笔重酬，而且不轻：只有我把看法交出来，您才肯让我读这部书。
接着他宣布，他在这里要扮两个角色：先作哲学家，再作神学家。一个人写反驳，先声明自己要换两副面孔。
末了他还加了一句：要是写得不好，那是您的错，是您逼我写的。
这封信，连同这几句抱怨，印在了笛卡尔自己的书里。

sections.heading: 作者自己说了为什么
paragraphs: 六个沉思前面，有一篇写给读者的序。用意他在那里就讲明了。
他说，我先在沉思里把我的想法摆出来，试一试同样这些道理，能不能也说服别人。然后我要答复几位才学出众的人的反驳，这几篇沉思付印之前，送给他们审过。
跟着就是那把锁：他们提的反驳又多又杂，我敢指望，别人再想到什么要紧的，不大会是他们还没碰过的。
所以他请读者，先别对这几篇沉思下判断，等把那些反驳和答复全都读过了再说。
照这个算法，对方的分量越足，他们没碰到的地方就越可以记作没有问题。一份手下留情的反对意见，它没说到的地方就不算数。

sections.heading: 他又用了两次
paragraphs: 答第四组的开头，他对着一个人又说了一遍。
他说阿尔诺逼得这样紧，紧到不必担心有人以为他碍着情面留了手；因此，我不太在意他反对的那些，倒是高兴他在更多地方没有反对。
答第五组里，他把它转了个方向。
他对伽桑狄说，我看您与其说是在驳我的道理，不如说是在用些辞令的巧劲绕开它们；而这一层我倒也领情，因为由此我可以推想，拿得出来跟前面别人那几组不一样的道理，本来就不容易。前面那几组，您是读过的。若真有，以您的机敏和用功，是漏不掉的。
他不是在说对方笨。他是反过来用：正因为对方足够厉害，对方没拿出新道理这件事，本身成了一条消息。厉害的人都找不到，他由此推想，那样的道理本来就不容易有。
序里是一群人又多又杂，答阿尔诺是一个人下手够狠，答伽桑狄是一个人够机敏。三处都把对方的本事，折算成了自己这边的凭据。
而要这么折算，得有个前提：对方真厉害，并且读者看得见他厉害。所以反驳得印出来，还得让人读到。他在序里请读者先读完反驳再下判断，为的正是这个。光说我经受住了考验没有用，考验本身得摆在纸上，让人自己掂它够不够重。

sections.heading: 没被挑出来的那些
paragraphs: 你把自己写的东西拿给人看，请对方提意见。
对方真提了，而且提得不客气。你去争那几条：哪一条不对，哪一条是误会。争完了，心里松一口气。
另一笔账是对方没提的那些。它没有形状，不刺眼，也不需要回应，所以容易不算。可它未必是零：一双认真找茬的眼睛看过去没有开口的地方，多少说明了一点东西。
说明多少，要看那双眼睛看到了哪里。只读了第一章的人没提第五章，什么也不说明。

sections.heading: 收束
paragraphs: 书里那个人，在火炉边一连想了几天。书外，稿子送出去请人来打，打的和挡的，一并印在了后头。那些来回的篇幅，远远超过前面那几天的沉思。
他给出了自己的判断：要紧的反驳，大概都已经在这里了。
他也把可能驳倒这个判断的材料，印进了同一本书。

notes: 主要依据拉丁文《致读者序》、答第四组开头、答第五组开头。对方未提出异议能够说明多少，与其实际审查的范围和力度有关；本文不据此宣告笛卡尔已经排除全部反对。
底稿的五倍篇幅比未注明计量口径，改为不依赖特定版本的规模对照。
zh.aside: 《SAE第一批判》里有一句，说别人的追问提供一种自问担保不了的校验；紧跟着一句写明，它不是唯一的校验。笛卡尔在序里说的比这多一步：追问的人又多又杂，要紧的大概都已经碰过了。这是旁注，不是论证。

title.en: Descartes, Œuvres VII: Preface and the Objections and Replies

zh_edits.old: 到第二版，篇幅是前面那几天的五倍不止。
zh_edits.new: 那些来回的篇幅，远远超过前面那几天的沉思。

en.title: He Asked for the Objections
en.deck: A severe critic can become evidence for the author—but only if the reader can see the criticism.

paragraphs: The usual order would have been simple. Publish a book. Wait for somebody to object. Answer them in another book. The exchange might take years and occupy several volumes.
Descartes arranged things differently. The objections were invited before the book went to press.

sections.heading: A letter that begins with a complaint
paragraphs: The Fourth Objections were written by Antoine Arnauld. They begin with a letter to Mersenne, and the letter begins by complaining: you would not give me this favour for nothing. You demanded a substantial payment—my opinion of the book—as the price of letting me read it.

Arnauld then announces two roles. First he will speak as a philosopher, then as a theologian. One critic, two declared capacities. At the end he adds that if the result is unsatisfactory, Mersenne must take the blame: Mersenne made him do it.
That letter, complaints included, was printed in Descartes’ own volume.

sections.heading: Why the author wanted them
paragraphs: Descartes explains his purpose in the preface to the reader. First he will set out his thoughts in the meditations, to test whether the reasons that convinced him can convince someone else. Then he will answer objections from learned readers who examined the manuscript before publication.

Next comes the tightening of the claim. The objections are so numerous and varied that he ventures to hope any important difficulty another reader might raise has probably already occurred to these critics. He asks readers to withhold judgment until they have read the objections and replies as well.

On that reckoning, a critic’s strength matters twice. It lends weight to what the critic challenges, and it lends some weight to what the critic leaves unchallenged. A deliberately gentle report would be useless for the second purpose: silence from someone who is holding back tells you very little.

sections.heading: Two more uses of the same move
paragraphs: At the beginning of the Fourth Replies, Descartes makes the point personally. Arnauld has pressed him hard enough that nobody need suspect indulgence. Descartes therefore takes less concern from the objections than satisfaction from the many things Arnauld did not object to.

In the Fifth Replies he turns the thought around. Gassendi, he says, seems less to refute the arguments than to evade their force through rhetorical ingenuity. Even that is useful. Given Gassendi’s ability and diligence, it suggests that genuinely new objections are not easy to find. Gassendi has read the preceding sets; had there been a different strong argument available, he would hardly have missed it.
This is not a charge of stupidity. The critic must be intelligent for the inference to work. An able opponent’s failure to produce a new reason is itself made into information.

In the preface, the test is the number and variety of the critics. With Arnauld, it is the severity of one reader. With Gassendi, it is one reader’s ingenuity. Each time, the opponent’s strength is converted into evidence on the author’s side.

But for that conversion to carry weight, the opponent must really be formidable—and the reader must be able to see it. The objections have to be printed. Simply announcing that the book survived examination is not enough. The examination itself must be on the page, where readers can decide how demanding it was.

sections.heading: The things nobody marked
paragraphs: You give someone a draft and ask for criticism. They oblige, and they are not gentle. You argue over the marked passages: this objection is mistaken; that one rests on a misunderstanding. Afterwards, you feel some relief.

There is another account to reckon with: everything they left unmarked. It does not sting, has no visible outline, and requires no reply, so it is easy to treat it as nothing. Yet a passage scrutinized by a serious critic without provoking an objection may tell you something.
How much it tells you depends on how far those eyes actually travelled. Someone who read only Chapter One tells you nothing by failing to complain about Chapter Five.

sections.heading: At the end
paragraphs: Inside the main text, a man sits by the fire and thinks over successive days. Outside it, a manuscript circulates, people attack it, and author and opponents are bound into the same volume. The exchanges occupy far more space than the initial meditations.
Descartes offers his own assessment: the important objections have probably been raised already. He also prints the material with which a reader might challenge that assessment.

en.aside: The SAE First Critique describes another person’s questioning as a check that self-questioning cannot guarantee, while explicitly declining to call it the only possible check. Descartes’ preface makes a stronger inference: so many varied critics have looked that the important difficulties have probably been encountered. Placing the claims beside each other does not prove either one.
notes: Principal passages: the Latin Preface to the Reader; the beginning of the Fourth Replies; the opening exchange of the Fifth Replies. This reading separates Descartes’ assessment of the objections from a verdict that his assessment is correct.
A fixed five-to-one length ratio is not retained: the textual scope and counting method were not specified in the manuscript. The contrast in scale remains.
